introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - Advanced Level Examination. Information and Communication Technologies (0796), Paper 3 (practical), June 2026. Duration: two hours. Answer ALL TASKS.**

The booklet reproduced here contains three versions of the same practical paper, headed Group 1, Group 2 and Group 3 (booklets 00/0796/3/G1, G2 and G3). Each version has two tasks, Task A (Databases, 28 marks) and Task B (Spreadsheet, 22 marks), on the same model, with different files, names, weights and cell references.

Enter the information required in the shaded boxes. Do not write in pencil. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answer. Your results must be recorded in the spaces provided in this question booklet. Candidates must allow for themselves enough time to complete and check their work where these are required. The supervisor will guide you on how to save your files but usually you will be expected to save all your work in one folder named *Candidate folder* that will be created in your desktop. When an imperative programming language is require to write program code, either Standard [ISO] Pascal or [ANSI] C programming language may be used. You should ensure all your work is collected and printed before leaving the examination room. All printed work should be inserted in this booklet and well stapled. Carefully handle all equipment put at your disposal to avoid accidents that may lead to a disaster or system failure. Report any case of system or device malfunction to your supervisor.

The working files (the database and the workbook of each group) are supplied on the day in the Candidate folder; they are not reproduced in the printed paper.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use formula and cell referencing wherever the formula requires a value found in the worksheet:

a) **Test Average**: This is calculated by taking into consideration the test mark and the weight of the exam (Exam Weight) found in row 20. It is done by taking the sum of the product of each test mark and the weight exam (found in row 20). For example, Test1*Exam Weight + Test2*Exam Weight....

Write down the formula you have used to calculate the test average for Awudu Mustapha in cell G4:

G4: ................................  *[2 marks]*

Used absolute reference in the appropriate reference in the above formula and copy the formula to other students. Write down the formula to derive the test average for Fred Jerry.

Fred Jerry: ................................  *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The weights are in **row 20**; the layout is assumed to be C20:F20 = weights of Test 1 to Test 4, in the same columns as the marks (Test 1 = 10%, Test 2 = 20%). The marks of the four tests are in C to F and the test average goes in column G (assumed layout, student rows 4 to 14). The test average is the sum of (mark x weight), so each mark is multiplied by the weight of its own test.

**First part, cell G4 (Awudu Mustapha, row 4):**

`G4: =C4*C20+D4*D20+E4*E20+F4*F20`

**Second part, Fred Jerry.** When the formula is copied down to the other students, the marks must move with the row (C4, C5...), but the weights must not move: they stay in the same cells for every student. The weight references are therefore made **absolute** with dollar signs (F4 key): `$C$20`, and so on. For a student on row n:

`=Cn*$C$20+Dn*$D$20+En*$E$20+Fn*$F$20`

The row of Fred Jerry is not given in the paper; if he is on row 12, for example, the formula is `=C12*$C$20+D12*$D$20+E12*$E$20+F12*$F$20`. An equivalent short form is `=SUMPRODUCT(C4:F4,$C$20:$F$20)`.

The weights are percentages that add up to 100%, so the test average stays on the same scale as the marks.

Check (invented marks and weights, not from the paper, run in Python): marks [56, 48, 62, 70] with weights 10%, 20%, 30%, 40% give 56*10% + 48*20% + 62*30% + 70*40% = **61.80**.

Marking idea (3 marks): marks multiplied by the weights of the right cells (1); all four tests added (1); weight references made absolute in the second formula (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) **Semester Average**: If the student's homework is **OK** then the semester average is the test average plus the homework bonus (HW Bonus) found in cell H17; otherwise, the semester average is just the test average. Apply absolute reference to your formula and copy the formula through the other students. Write down the formula you have used to calculate the commission for Becky Sanda in cell I8:

I8: ................................  *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(The word "commission" is a misprint of the paper: the cell I8 holds the **semester average**.)

The decision needs a conditional formula (`IF`). The student's homework status is read in column H of the student's row (assumed layout: "OK" when the homework is done properly), the test average in column G, and the bonus in H17, which is the same for every student and so is written as an absolute reference `$H$17`.

`I8: =IF(H8="OK",G8+$H$17,G8)`

- If `H8="OK"` is true, the result is the test average plus the bonus: `G8+$H$17`.
- Otherwise the result is the test average alone: `G8`.

Copied down column I, the row references (H, G) change with the student and `$H$17` stays fixed. The text "OK" is written between double quotation marks.

Check (invented data, run in Python): test average 61.80 with homework OK and a bonus of 2 gives **63.80**; with homework not OK it stays **61.80**.

Marking idea (3 marks): IF function with a test on the homework (1); correct result when OK, test average plus bonus (1); otherwise the test average, and the bonus cell made absolute (1).

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) **Grades**: If the semester mark of a student is between 0 to 40, his/her grade is D, 41 to 50 his/her grade is C, etc. Use conditional formula to insert the grade of the students by considering the semester average and grading scheme of test marks given in the range A25:C28.

Write down the formula used to obtain the Grade of Bah John in J7

J7: ................................  *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The grading scheme is in **A25:C28**. Assumed layout (the scheme is not reproduced in the paper): column A = lowest mark of the band, column B = highest mark, column C = grade, in ascending order, so row 25 is D (0 to 40), row 26 is C (41 to 50), and so on up to row 28, the best grade. Bah John's semester average is in I7 (the grade goes in column J, row 7).

A conditional formula tests the best band first and goes down; the limits and the grades are read from the scheme with absolute references (they must not move when the formula is copied down):

`J7: =IF(I7>=$A$28,$C$28,IF(I7>=$A$27,$C$27,IF(I7>=$A$26,$C$26,$C$25)))`

Reading: if the semester average is at least the lower limit of the top band (`$A$28`), the grade is `$C$28`; otherwise the next band is tested, and so on; if no other band applies, the grade is `$C$25` (the 0 to 40 band).

An equivalent formula uses the approximate look-up on the scheme: `=VLOOKUP(I7,$A$25:$C$28,3,TRUE)` (the fourth argument TRUE, or omitted, searches the largest lower limit that is not above the average, which requires column A in ascending order). If the scheme is stored in the opposite order in the real workbook (best grade first), the references of the nested IF are simply taken in the other order.

Because the limits of the scheme are whole numbers, a decimal average such as 40.5 is below the lower limit 41 of band C and receives grade D with both formulas.

Check (invented bands for the test only: the paper gives only D for 0 to 40 and C for 41 to 50; B from 51 and A from 61 are assumed here; both formulas simulated in Python on 0, 0.5, 1 ... 100 and found equal), semester average -> grade: 0 -> D, 38 -> D, 40 -> D, 41 -> C, 50 -> C, 51 -> B, 60 -> B, 61 -> A, 100 -> A. The invented semester average 63.80 gives grade **A**.

Marking idea (3 marks): IF (or equivalent) used with the semester average (1); the limits taken from the scheme range (1); all the grades produced correctly, with absolute references (1).

Write down a formula you used to calculate the class average of Test 3 in cell E16:

The class average of a test is the average of all the marks of that test: the function **AVERAGE** on the column of the test. Test 3 is in column E (assumed layout), student rows 4 to 14:

`E16: =AVERAGE(E4:E14)`

What matters is the range of the marks of the test, not the cell that receives the result. Copy the formula to the cells of the other tests (the column letter changes by itself); the range must stop at row 14 so that it does not include the statistics rows.

Check (invented marks of one test [52, 61, 47, 70, 38, 55, 66, 49, 58, 63, 44], run in Python): the average is **54.82**.

Marking idea (2 marks): function AVERAGE (1); correct range of the marks of the test (1).

g) **Grade Count**: Use formula to count the number of occurrences of each grade in the J column.

Enter the formula in the range H25:H28.

Write down the formula you have used to count the number of occurrences for

Grade A in H25: ................................

Grade D in H25: ................................  *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The grades are in column J (J4:J14). The function **COUNTIF** counts the cells of a range that satisfy a condition; the range is absolute so that the formulas can be copied down the four cells of H25:H28:

`H25: =COUNTIF($J$4:$J$14,"A")`

`H28: =COUNTIF($J$4:$J$14,"D")`

The paper prints "Grade D in H25", but H25 is already used for grade A: grade D, the fourth grade, is counted in H28. The condition can also be the cell that holds the grade letter next to the count, which lets the same formula be copied for B and C.

Check (invented grades ACBDCBACBAD in J4:J14, run in Python): A = 3, B = 3, C = 3, D = 2; the four counts add up to 11, the number of students.

Marking idea (2 marks): COUNTIF on the J column for A (1); the same for D (1).
